summary: This informational RFC looks at the technical side of blocking and filtering Internet services. It describes common approaches and discusses their effects on the network and on users, including unintended side effects and ways they can be bypassed, to help policy makers and engineers understand the trade-offs.

plainLanguage.summary: This document looks at how blocking and filtering of Internet services are actually carried out, and what each method costs. It finds that every approach breaks something else, and that filtering done by the user's own software does the least damage.

questions: side effects of blocking internet services
how is internet filtering carried out in practice
what is the difference between blocking and filtering
subtitle: Technical trade-offs and consequences of blocking and filtering Internet services.

tldr.problem: Governments, enterprises and operators increasingly block or filter Internet services, and each method has side effects that hit people and services the block was never aimed at.
tldr.mechanism: The document classifies blocking systems by who sets the policy, what they are for, what they target and which part of the Internet they act on, then evaluates three design patterns against scope, granularity, efficacy and security.
tldr.outcome: Its conclusion is that filtering should be done at the endpoint whenever possible, that there are no good technical solutions and only least bad ones, and that a hybrid of endpoint and network filtering may be the least damaging.

facts.label: Service components
facts.value: 3: endpoints, network services and rendezvous services

today: RFC 7754 is an Informational document published by the Internet Architecture Board, with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it remains the standing analysis of blocking and filtering techniques. Its conclusions are advisory: it offers no rules to follow and no formulas for weighing the trade-offs, and it leaves the legal and ethical questions outside its scope.

sections.title: Why the IAB Wrote This
sections.content:
The original design goal of the Internet was to enable communications between hosts. As people began using it to communicate, it became apparent that some hosts were engaging in communications viewed as undesirable by certain parties; the most famous early example is the Morris worm, which used the Internet to infect many hosts in 1988. Mechanisms to restrict such communications have grown alongside the Internet, ranging from acceptable use policies enforced through informal channels to technical blocking mechanisms.

Efforts to restrict or deny access to Internet resources and services have evolved over time. Some Internet service providers perform filtering to restrict which applications their customers may use and which traffic they allow, often with customer consent, where the customers may be enterprises or individuals. However, governments, service providers and enterprises are increasingly seeking to block or filter access to certain content, traffic or services without the knowledge or agreement of affected users, and where these organizations do not directly control networks they commonly aim to make use of intermediary systems.

The document notes that the difference between blocking and filtering is a matter of scale and perspective. Blocking often refers to preventing access to resources in the aggregate, while filtering refers to preventing access to specific resources within an aggregate. Both can be implemented at the level of services, such as web hosting or video streaming, or at the level of particular content. For the analysis the two terms are treated as generally equivalent.

The aim is to clarify the technical implications and trade-offs of blocking strategies and to identify the potential for harmful side effects, called collateral damage, for Internet users and for the Internet architecture itself. The scope is limited to technical blocking mechanisms and to intentional blocking, not accidental blocking caused by misconfiguration or as a side effect of something else. Whether particular forms of filtering are lawful or ethical in a given place is out of scope; the document is written for those who are doing the filtering or considering doing it.
sections.plainLanguage: The document exists because blocking has become common and each way of doing it has consequences that are easy to overlook. It sets aside the legal and moral questions and looks only at the engineering: what a block actually breaks, and for whom.

sections.title: How Blocking Is Done Today
sections.content:
Blocking systems have evolved alongside the Internet technologies they seek to restrict. Firewalls of various sorts are very commonly employed, either on end hosts under user or administrator control or in the network at network boundaries. Informally most people think of a firewall as something that blocks unwanted traffic, and three specific types of functionality are worth noting. Stateless packet filtering blocks according to content-neutral rules, for example blocking all outbound connections on certain ports, protocols or network-layer addresses, such as blocking outbound connections to port 25. Stateful packet filtering keeps state in order to enforce flow-based policies, such as blocking inbound traffic for flows that have not been established. Deep packet inspection filters or blocks based on the content carried.

Web filtering targets specific URIs in HTTP and HTTPS. Some enterprises use HTTP blocking to block non-work-appropriate sites, and several nations require HTTP and HTTPS filtering by their ISPs. HTTPS is a challenge because the URI is carried inside the encrypted channel, so a filtering system must either block on network- and transport-layer headers, meaning IP address and or port, or obtain a trust anchor certificate trusted by endpoints and act as a man in the middle. Such systems often take the form of portals or enterprise proxies presenting their own dynamically generated HTTPS certificates.

Spam filtering is one of the oldest forms of content filtering. Spam filters evaluate messages against a variety of criteria and information sources, for example using reverse DNS to flag whether an IP address is a known spam source. They can be installed on user devices, operated by a mail domain on behalf of users, or outsourced to a third party acting as an intermediate mail exchanger. Domain name seizure uses approaches such as the Uniform Dispute Resolution Policy of ICANN, or a requirement from another authority that domains be blocked within a jurisdiction. The precise method varies from place to place; in some cases the person whose name was seized simply uses a new name, and in others the block is effective only within a region or only when particular name service infrastructure is used. Seizures can also have overbroad effects, since access to content is blocked not only within the jurisdiction of the seizure but globally, even when it may be legal elsewhere. Where redirection is effected at intermediate resolvers rather than authoritative servers, it directly contradicts end-to-end assumptions in the DNS security architecture, potentially causing validation failures by validating end-nodes.

Safe browsing is provided by modern web browsers: before loading a URI, current versions of Google Chrome and Firefox use the Google Safe Browsing service to determine whether a given URI is safe to load, and the DNS can also be used to store third party information marking domains as safe or unsafe. Manipulation of routing and addressing data has been used by governments to maintain control over a specific set of DNS servers, as in the internationally coordinated response to the DNSChanger malware, where a Dutch court ordered the RIPE NCC to freeze the accounts of several resource holders to limit their ability to use certain address blocks. This has raised concerns that the number resource certification system and the secure routing technologies developed by the IETF's SIDR working group might be subject to the same manipulation. Ingress filtering is used by network service providers to prevent source address spoofing. Data loss prevention tools address the risk of confidential information leaking, and enterprise proxies may be part of such a solution.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists the techniques in use: firewalls that look at addresses and ports, filters that read inside web requests, spam filters, blocking of domain names, safe-browsing lists built into browsers, manipulation of routing data, source address checks, and tools that stop information leaking out.

sections.title: The Pieces a Blocking System Has
sections.content:
At a generic level, blocking systems can be characterised by four attributes: the party who sets the blocking policy, the purpose of the blocking, the intended target of the blocking, and the Internet components used as the basis of the blocking system.

The party setting the policy may be a government, court, enterprise, network operator, reputation tracker, application provider or individual end user. There are several steps of translation and transformation from the original intended purpose, first to laws, then to regulation, then to high-level policies in network operators, and from those to filtering architecture and implementation, and each step is a potential source of unintended consequences. Sometimes the policy setter is also the enforcer, such as a network operator installing a firewall in its own equipment or a web application provider blocking responses between its web server and certain clients. Often they differ: the policy may be imposed on the enforcing entity, as with government-initiated blocking, or the enforcing entity may choose to use policy set by others, as with a reputation system used by a spam filter or a safe browsing service. Because a policy might be enforced by others, it is best if it can be expressed in a form independent of the enforcing technology.

The purposes of blocking fall into three groups. Preventing or responding to security threats, since operators, enterprises, application providers and end users often block communications believed to be associated with security threats or network attacks. Restricting objectionable content or services, whether because a government considers something defamatory, hate speech, obscene or infringing intellectual property, or an enterprise restricts employees from content that is not work appropriate, or parents restrict children from adult content. And restricting access based on business arrangements, where some networks are designed to offer only certain content, walled gardens, or only limited access until the user pays, as with captive portals provided by hotspot operators. The purpose often dictates the model: captive portals, walled gardens and sandboxes used for security or network endpoint assessment need a whitelist model, where communications are blocked by default and only a subset allowed, while blocking for other purposes often uses a blacklist model, where communications are allowed by default and only a subset blocked.

Broadly speaking, delivering an Internet service involves three components. Endpoints are the actual content of the service, typically an application-layer protocol between two or more hosts, in many protocols a client and a server. Network services are the IP networks the endpoints use, with routing protocols determining how packets are delivered between them. Rendezvous services let one endpoint work out how to contact another from an identifier more human-friendly than an IP address; the domain name system is the example, and distributed hash tables have also been used.

The worked example is an HTTP transaction fetching http://example.com/index.html. The client endpoint is an end host running a browser. The client uses the DNS as a rendezvous service when it performs an AAAA query to obtain the IP address for the server name, then establishes a connection and sends the HTTP request, and the server endpoint responds. The same request could have been prevented in several ways: by preventing the client from making the request, by preventing the server from responding, by preventing the client from making the DNS request, by preventing the request or the response from reaching its destination, by preventing the client from reaching the DNS servers or the DNS responses from reaching the client, or by preventing the DNS servers from providing the client with the correct IP address of the server.

Those who want to block typically have access to only one or two of these components, which limits their choices. End users and application providers control only their own software and hardware, so they are limited to endpoint-based filtering, though some network operators offer filtering services their customers can switch on individually. Network operators control their own networks and the rendezvous services for which they provide infrastructure or to which they have access, such as DNS resolvers or SIP proxies, but not usually endpoints. Enterprises usually have their own networks and endpoints. Governments might make arrangements with the operators or owners of any of the three components within their jurisdictions.
sections.plainLanguage: Any service on the Internet has three parts: the programs at each end, the networks that carry the traffic, and the directories or databases that help one end find the other. A block works by attacking one of the three, and whoever wants to block usually controls only one or two of them.

sections.title: Three Ways to Block, and What Each Costs
sections.content:
The three design patterns are evaluated against four criteria. Scope asks which hosts and users are affected: blocking within an access network affects only the users connected to it, while blocking performed by an application provider can affect users across the entire Internet. Blocking systems are less objectionable when the scope is as narrow as possible while still effective, and when the impact stays inside the administrative realm of the policy setter. Design flaws can make effects overbroad: the document cites a provider that blocked content under a regulation and ended up blocking it for downstream providers in other jurisdictions, and others that leaked such black hole routes beyond the jurisdiction.

Granularity asks how specific the blocking is and whether blocking one service also blocks others. Applications are built from loosely coupled layers developed autonomously and run by different parties, so an action at one layer can affect another, and manipulating routing or naming to restrict access affects every application that depends on those functions. Blocking all traffic of one application protocol is less granular than blocking a subset of application instances, and heuristics using the application protocol, payload signatures, addresses, inter-packet timing and packet sizes are sometimes used to narrow the subset.

Efficacy asks how easily a resource can avoid being blocked. A one-time policy is often unlikely to last, and blacklisting needs continual maintenance of the list in both directions, adding entries for unwanted traffic and removing them when the offending content goes. Because Internet resources are distributed and mobile, a service blocked in one jurisdiction can often be moved or re-instantiated in another, services that rely on blocked resources can be reconfigured quickly, and content can move to another name or address or use alternate syntaxes. A technique called snowshoe spamming uses addresses in many networks as spam sources, spreading it across jurisdictions.

Users and applications can also change their behaviour: shifting to port 80 or 443 when other ports are blocked, tunnelling a service inside another, proxying through a collaborating external host, or running over an alternate port such as 8080 instead of 80. Filtering systems that identify only IPv4 traffic can be evaded by shifting to IPv6, and IPv6 with header options or encrypted tunnels make ports harder to find inside packets.

Security asks how the blocking affects existing trust infrastructures. Protocols such as TLS and IPsec are designed so each endpoint knows the other's identity and only the endpoints can read the content. Some blocking strategies need intermediaries inside the end-to-end path, potentially breaking those properties, and it can then be impossible for endpoints to tell attackers from authorised parties doing the blocking.

Network-based blocking uses intermediary devices that inspect traffic as it passes. Many of its problems come from an intermediary needing enough traffic to make its determinations: the Internet delivers packets independently rather than to a chosen point, so a packet sequence can only be reconstructed reliably at the intended receiver, and inter-network routing is often asymmetric. An intermediary may see only half a conversation, so a filter aimed at requests for particular URIs cannot decide from the URI if it is only in the path for responses.

On granularity, deep packet inspection can be narrower and less damaging than blocking all traffic to an address, but narrow targeting may be more complex or easier to circumvent. On efficacy, IP addresses stay visible even when packets are protected with IPsec, and blocking on addresses is trivial to circumvent because a filtered site can change its address by editing one DNS record. If content is encrypted with IPsec or TLS, the intermediary must decrypt the packets or guess statistically, and since security protocols are designed to keep intermediaries out, it would have to masquerade as one of the endpoints, breaking authentication and reducing security for the users affected. Techniques that use public databases of whitelisted keys, such as DANE, let users detect these intermediaries, and those users are then likely to act as if the service is blocked.

The document then observes that in principle it is impossible to block tunnelled traffic through an intermediary without blocking all secure traffic from that system, the only practical limitation being the need for special software on the client. The longer such systems run, the more likely efficient tunnelling tools become, so network-based blocking weakens over time. It is a key contributor to an arms race that creates unnecessary complexity: port blocking pushed applications to ports 80 and 443, which pushed operators to content blocking over port 80, which pushed providers to encrypted channels, which pushed operators to hunt for those channels. The reason is fundamental: the Internet was designed on the premise that people will want to connect, so nearly any authorised path can serve as a transport.

Rendezvous-based blocking targets global services such as the DNS, certificate authorities, search engines, WHOIS databases and Internet Route Registries, which register the structure and availability of applications. Because many application-layer services rely on generic global databases, the effects of changing them are harder to predict than shutting down a web server. A block at a global rendezvous service can deny services in jurisdictions where they are considered legitimate, and collateral damage is lessened when blocking happens at a local rendezvous server with only local impact. Its efficacy is limited by the distributed nature of the Internet: local networks can patch the authoritative data, though DNSSEC and the RPKI are changing that by requiring authorised updates, and registrants can relocate resources to other names. Endpoints can also decline to use a particular rendezvous service, using IP literals in URIs to get around DNS filtering. The document's summary of the pattern adapts a quotation: the Internet treats blocking as damage and routes around it.

Three examples are given. In 2008 Pakistan Telecom tried to deny YouTube inside Pakistan by announcing bogus routes for YouTube address space to its peers; YouTube was denied service globally because of a route leak beyond the ISP's scope, and service was restored in approximately two hours when operators elsewhere reconfigured their routers to ignore the bogus routes. In the DNS, United States law enforcement seizing names involved a Spanish web site: although several affected names belonged to Spanish organisations, they were blocked because certain servers were operated in the United States, and officials required the operators of the parent zones to direct queries to United States government-operated name servers, so users of other services under that name could no longer find the servers providing them. The Dutch authorities' action against the RIPE NCC, freezing the accounts of Internet resource holders, limited how those ISPs could manage their resources by controlling account holders' WHOIS information; it did not immediately affect connectivity, because use of WHOIS for route filters is voluntary, but it may affect trust in the shared infrastructure.

Endpoint-based blocking works because users and their devices constantly decide whether to engage in particular communications: whether to click a link in a suspect email, whether a browser warns against a site with suspicious characteristics, whether a spam filter judges a message valid. If the software making those decisions can be told not to engage, the communications are effectively blocked because they never happen. The effects are usually local in scope, and endpoint-based blocking can see into the entire application, across all layers and transactions, giving it a much richer basis for narrow decisions, though how fine-grained it can be depends on how the client and server are designed.

It handles a mobile adversary better than the other two, because it can detect when a blocked service's resources have changed and adjust as quickly as a reputation system delivers new data. Its main challenge is that it needs the endpoint's cooperation: where cooperation is willing the barrier is low, needing only reconfiguration or a software update, and where it is unwilling it is hard to enforce across large numbers of endpoints. It avoids the end-to-end security problems of network-based blocking and the trust problems of rendezvous-based blocking. If a service is to be blocked, the best way of doing it is to disable the service at the server endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: Three methods are compared. Blocking inside the network can break encryption, sees only part of any conversation, and is easily routed around. Blocking at the directory or registry level reaches services in other countries too, and can be undone by local workarounds. Blocking at the user's own software is the narrowest and safest, but it needs the user's cooperation, which cannot be forced.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The primary security concern with Internet service blocking is its effect on the end-to-end security model of many Internet security protocols. When blocking is enforced by an intermediary, the blocking system may need access to confidentiality-protected data to make its decisions, and the mechanisms for obtaining such access often require defeating the authentication mechanisms built into those protocols.

Some enterprise firewalls dynamically create TLS certificates under a trust anchor recognised by the endpoints behind them. Those certificates let the firewall authenticate as any web site, so it can act as a man in the middle on TLS connections passing through it, which is not unlike an external attacker using compromised certificates to intercept TLS connections. Modifications of this kind make the firewall itself an attack surface: if an attacker gains control of the firewall or compromises the key pair it uses to sign certificates, the attacker gains access to the unencrypted data of all current and recorded TLS sessions for all users behind that firewall, in a way that is undetectable to users. If the compromised key pairs can be extracted from the firewall, all users who rely on that public key are vulnerable, not only those behind the firewall.

A legitimate administrator of such a firewall could also gain access to privacy-sensitive information, such as the bank accounts or health records of users who reach secure sites through the firewall. Those privacy considerations motivate legitimate use of secure end-to-end protocols, which is exactly what makes granular blocking policies hard to enforce. When blocking systems cannot inspect and surgically block secure protocols, it is tempting to block those protocols entirely; a web blocking system that cannot inspect HTTPS connections might simply block any attempted HTTPS connection. But since Internet security protocols are commonly used for critical services such as online commerce and banking, blocking them would block access to those services as well, or worse, force them to be conducted over insecure communication. Security protocols can also be used as blocking mechanisms, for example by inserting invalid credentials so that the other end terminates the connection on authentication failure, but it is typically much simpler to block secure protocols outright than to exploit them for service blocking.
sections.plainLanguage: The security section is about what it costs to break into encrypted traffic. A filter that wants to read HTTPS has to pretend to be the website, which turns the filtering device into a security liability, and blocking HTTPS outright takes banking and commerce down with it.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
Filtering will continue to occur on the Internet. The document concludes that whenever possible filtering should be done on the endpoint, because cooperative endpoints are most likely to have the contextual knowledge needed to target blocking effectively, and such blocking minimises unintended consequences. It is realistic to expect that at times filtering will not be done on the endpoints; in those cases, promptly informing the endpoint that blocking has occurred provides the transparency needed to redress errors, particularly errors relating to collateral damage from errant filters.

Blacklist approaches are often a game of cat and mouse, with those holding the content moving it around to avoid blocking, or the content being naturally mirrored or cached at other legitimate sites such as the Internet Archive Wayback Machine. Whitelists carry similar risks, because sites that had acceptable content may become targets for unacceptable content, and access to perfectly inoffensive and perhaps useful or productive content is unnecessarily blocked.

From a technical perspective there are no perfect or even good solutions, only least bad ones. On that front the document puts forward a hybrid approach that combines endpoint-based filtering with network filtering as the least damaging: an endpoint may choose to participate in a filtering regime in exchange for the network providing broader unfiltered access. Finally, where filtering is occurring to address content generally agreed to be inappropriate or illegal, strong cooperation among service providers and governments may provide additional means to identify both the victims and the perpetrators through non-filtering mechanisms, such as partnerships with the finance industry to identify and limit illegal transactions.
sections.plainLanguage: The conclusion is that filters belong on the user's own device whenever that is possible, and that when it is not, the user should at least be told. There is no good solution, only a choice of the least bad one, and a mix of endpoint and network filtering may be the least damaging of all.

viz.caption: The blocking and filtering techniques described in Section 2

items.title: Stateless packet filtering
items.text: Content-neutral rules, such as blocking outbound connections on certain ports.

items.title: Stateful packet filtering
items.text: Keeps state to enforce policies on flows, such as blocking traffic for flows that were never established.

items.title: Deep packet inspection
items.text: Filters on the content carried inside the packets.

items.title: Web filtering
items.text: Targets specific URIs in HTTP and HTTPS, often through a proxy that presents its own certificates.

items.title: Spam filtering
items.text: Evaluates messages against criteria such as reverse DNS reputation of the sending address.

items.title: Domain name seizure
items.text: Blocks or redirects a domain name; effects can reach beyond the jurisdiction that ordered it.

items.title: Safe browsing
items.text: A service consulted by browsers before loading a URI, with the DNS also able to carry safe or unsafe lists.

items.title: Ingress filtering
items.text: Checks source addresses at the edge of a network to prevent address spoofing.

viz.caption: The three components that deliver an Internet service

children.label: Endpoints
children.note: The application-layer protocol and its data.

children.label: Network services
children.note: IP networks and the routing protocols that deliver packets.

children.label: Rendezvous services
children.note: Directories that let one endpoint find another.

viz.caption: The three design patterns against the four criteria

cells: Whatever the intermediary can see, often only part of a communication because routing is asymmetric.
Global services, so a block in one jurisdiction can deny service in another.
Usually local, affecting only the user or the organisation that deployed it.
Deep packet inspection can be narrow, but it can only use what the intermediary can decrypt or guess.
Overbroad when the blocked name or address also hosts legitimate services.
Can see every layer and transaction, so it can target narrowly.
Circumventable by changing addresses, ports or tunnels; gets weaker as tunnelling tools improve.
Can be patched locally, and resources move quickly to other names and addresses.
Deals well with a mobile adversary, but needs the endpoint's cooperation.
May break end-to-end security by impersonating an endpoint.
Can erode trust in the shared infrastructure and encourage parallel networks.
Avoids both the end-to-end and the global trust problems.
